title: Milestones of AI History
brief: Trace how artificial intelligence grew from a bold parlor game into systems that beat world champions. Along the way, explore the hype cycles, dead ends, and hard-won lessons that shaped the field.

questions.question: In 1950, why did Alan Turing replace the question of whether machines can think with his imitation game?
questions.answer: Turing thought words like think and machine were too vague to test cleanly. Instead, he judged intelligence by observable behavior in a blind text conversation with a human. If a judge could not tell the machine from a person, it passed the test.
key_points: Asking if machines think is too vague to test, or he wanted to judge observable behavior instead
In the game, a judge chats over text and tries to tell the machine from a person
It shifted AI from arguing about inner consciousness to testing practical performance
questions.hint: Picture trying to peer inside someone's skull versus simply watching how they act.
questions.fun_fact: Turing modeled his famous test on a party game where a judge tried to tell a hidden man and woman apart using only typed notes.

questions.question: What is an AI winter, and what usually triggers one?
questions.answer: An AI winter is a long stretch when funding, research interest, and public optimism dry up. It usually begins after big hype and bold promises collide with real-world limits. Once systems disappoint backers, governments and companies pull their money and walk away.
key_points: A period when AI funding, attention, and research activity sharply drop
Triggered when overhyped promises fail to deliver working results
AI suffered two major winters in the seventies and late eighties
questions.hint: Imagine investors pouring cash into a wild forecast, then freezing out the whole field if the magic stalls.
questions.fun_fact: The 1956 Dartmouth workshop that named artificial intelligence actually proposed solving major parts of human intelligence with ten researchers in a single two-month summer.

questions.question: Why did early symbolic AI systems built on hand-written human rules break down in the messy real world?
questions.answer: Hand-coded rules worked well in tidy domains, yet they were painfully brittle outside narrow scripts. Real life is full of unwritten common sense, edge cases, and fuzzy exceptions. Programmers could never list every rule by hand, so the field shifted toward learning from data.
key_points: Rigid rules could not handle unwritten common sense and unexpected edge cases, or humans could never hand-code every real-world exception
Engineers called this sharp failure outside narrow domains brittleness
That wall pushed AI away from hand-written logic toward learning patterns from data
questions.hint: Try making an exact checklist for spotting a cat in any lighting or awkward pose.
questions.fun_fact: Starting in 1984, the Cyc project spent decades manually typing millions of basic facts like water makes things wet just to give software common sense.

questions.question: Why did Minsky and Papert's 1969 book stall neural networks, and how did backpropagation break that logjam?
questions.answer: Minsky and Papert proved single-layer networks could not solve simple nonlinear puzzles like exclusive or. Researchers lacked a practical way to train deeper networks, so neural network funding collapsed. Backpropagation fixed this by sending error signals backward to adjust weights inside hidden layers.
key_points: It proved single-layer networks could not solve simple nonlinear problems like exclusive or, or that researchers lacked a way to train deeper layers
Backpropagation passed error signals backward through the network to update hidden layers
A 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams popularized it and revived neural network research
questions.hint: One flat sheet could only draw a straight line, and nobody knew how to assign blame to the middle steps.
questions.fun_fact: Graduate student Paul Werbos actually worked out backpropagation for neural networks in his 1974 Harvard doctoral thesis, twelve years before the 1986 paper made it famous.

questions.concept: AlexNet and the deep learning boom
questions.question: What unlocked AlexNet's shock 2012 ImageNet win, and why did it transform computer vision?
questions.answer: AlexNet paired fast gaming graphics chips with over a million labeled photos to train a deep network. It beat traditional systems by more than ten percentage points on the top-five error score. That huge gap proved neural networks could learn visual features better than hand-coded vision rules.
key_points: Combining graphics chips with huge labeled image data to train a deep neural network
It crushed hand-crafted vision approaches by a wide margin, proving networks could learn visual features themselves
It dropped the contest error rate from about 26 percent to roughly 15 percent
questions.hint: Imagine silicon built to render virtual worlds meeting a giant tagged picture library, leaving old custom-built filters in the dust.
questions.fun_fact: Alex Krizhevsky trained AlexNet inside his bedroom at his parents' house using just two consumer gaming graphics cards.

questions.question: Why did AlphaGo beat world champion Lee Sedol a decade early when chess-style brute-force search failed at Go?
questions.answer: Go has far too many legal moves and subtle board patterns for brute-force search alone. AlphaGo paired tree search with two neural networks that learned promising moves and winning positions. Its successor, AlphaGo Zero, even skipped human games and mastered Go purely through self-play.
key_points: AlphaGo paired tree search with neural networks that learned intuition for promising moves and board values
Go's enormous branching factor and subtle positions made pure brute-force calculation impossible
A year later, AlphaGo Zero ditched human game records and surpassed it purely through self-play
questions.hint: Instead of checking every path mechanically, picture blending look-ahead planning with a trained gut feel.
questions.fun_fact: In game two against Lee Sedol, AlphaGo played a stunning move that its own software estimated only one in 10,000 human players would pick.

questions.question: According to Moravec's paradox, why is mastering chess or calculus easier for AI than walking and grabbing objects like a toddler?
questions.answer: Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing animal sight, balance, and physical movement. Those skills feel effortless only because huge hidden brain circuits run them automatically. Abstract math and board games are recent human add-ons with tidy rules that computers copy easily.
key_points: Evolution spent millions of years building massive subconscious brain power for sight and movement, or formal logic is a simpler recent add-on
Perception and motor control feel effortless to us only because our brains run them automatically
Formal games and math follow neat rules that are far easier to program than messy physical skills
questions.hint: Compare how long nature practiced catching prey versus how long people have studied algebra.
questions.fun_fact: Psychologist Steven Pinker summed up early AI history with one neat twist: the hard problems turned out easy, and the easy problems turned out hard.

questions.question: In Richard Sutton's famous essay The Bitter Lesson, why do general search and learning methods keep beating clever human-crafted rules?
questions.answer: Computing power grows exponentially over time, and general methods get stronger with every wave of faster hardware. Hand-built human insights help in the short run, yet they plateau and block bigger discoveries. Sutton calls this bitter because researchers hate watching their clever domain tricks lose to raw scale.
key_points: Computing power keeps growing exponentially, so general search and learning methods keep improving with more compute
Human-crafted domain rules bring short-term gains but hit a ceiling and cannot match open-ended scaling
Sutton called the lesson bitter because researchers dislike seeing hand-built expertise overtaken by raw computation
questions.hint: Ask yourself which ingredient doubles every couple of years while our minds stay flat.
questions.fun_fact: Sutton wrote his essay in 2019 using chess, Go, speech recognition, and computer vision as proof, years before giant language models made scaling famous.
